paragraphs: Approximating a function accurately does not necessarily mean reproducing its smooth behavior. A neural network can give values close to the target while still changing sharply around those values. This paper studies that gap for convolutional residual networks, connecting their ability to represent functions with control over their first-order smoothness.

The authors prove that sufficiently large ConvResNets can approximate target function values while also meeting a first-order smoothness requirement. This strengthens the kind of approximation guarantee described in the abstract: the network's behavior between nearby inputs matters alongside the accuracy of its outputs. They also extend the analysis to functions supported on a low-dimensional manifold.

The results offer a partial theoretical explanation for the practical benefits of deep and wide networks. They concern what sufficiently large networks can represent, rather than establishing that every trained large network will be smooth or robust. Experiments involving adversarially robust image classification support the theory and connect its approximation perspective to a practical learning problem.
icml-2022-benefits-of-overparameterized-.tldr: Large convolutional residual networks can approximate function values while maintaining first-order smoothness, partially explaining benefits of overparameterization.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a simple modification to graph inputs: adding a dummy node connected to every existing vertex. The original vertices and edges retain their properties. The goal is to strengthen graph structure learning while providing a theoretical explanation for the modification, rather than relying only on an architectural choice that works in practice.

The authors prove that the additional node supports an efficient transformation from edges to vertices, together with an inverse that recovers the original graph. The analysis indicates that the construction can preserve both local and global structure. This gives the added node a structural role beyond simply introducing another place for a model to aggregate information.

The authors incorporate dummy nodes into graph kernels and graph neural networks, testing graph classification and subgraph isomorphism matching. Their experiments report significant improvements when models receive the augmented graphs, with similar results from the corresponding edge-to-vertex graphs. They also discuss increased neural-network expressive power, linking the empirical gains to how graph structure can be represented.
icml-2022-boosting-graph-structure-learn.tldr: Adding a universally connected dummy node supports structure-preserving graph transformations and improves graph learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: CITRIS aims to recover the hidden causal factors behind a changing visual scene. It learns from image sequences in which those factors may have been intervened upon. Its key sources of information are how observations evolve over time and which underlying factors are known to have been targeted by interventions.

The framework uses a variational autoencoder to learn causal representations, including factors with multiple components, such as three-dimensional rotation angles. The authors prove identifiability in a setting that allows an intervention to affect only some components of a factor. A normalizing-flow extension also lets CITRIS separate causal factors within representations supplied by an already pretrained autoencoder.

On rendered three-dimensional image sequences, CITRIS recovers underlying causal variables better than the previous methods evaluated. With pretrained autoencoders, it can also generalize to unseen instantiations of causal factors. These findings suggest a route toward broader causal representation learning, while the abstract presents transfer from simulation to reality as a future research direction rather than an established result.
icml-2022-citris-causal-identifiability-.tldr: CITRIS combines temporal images and observed intervention targets to identify scalar and multidimensional causal factors.

paragraphs: A targeted adversarial attack must achieve two things together: make a chosen class more probable than every alternative, and keep the altered input within an allowed distance of the original. This paper develops white-box attacks whose optimization objectives more directly express those requirements. White-box access is part of the setting studied.

The first contribution is a loss function that explicitly represents the target-class ranking objective. Using it with Auto-PGD produces more successful attacks. The authors then refine the loss to incorporate the perturbation bound and introduce Constrained Gradient Descent. CGD handles misclassification and the bounded norm within its optimization, instead of relying on projection or clipping as post-processing.

The reported evaluations find greater attack success on CIFAR10 and ImageNet while using less time than the compared state-of-the-art attacks. Statistical tests also support improvements against leading defenses across different datasets and perturbation allowances. The findings show that aligning the optimization with both attack requirements can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of these evaluated robustness tests.
icml-2022-constrained-gradient-descent-a.tldr: Constrained Gradient Descent jointly optimizes targeted misclassification and perturbation bounds, improving attack success and runtime in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning seeks policies that satisfy specified constraints before deployment. This paper approaches that problem through probabilistic inference, responding to instability and missing optimality guarantees in earlier primal-dual approaches. Its central idea is to separate finding a suitable constrained distribution from updating the parameterized policy that will act.

The method alternates two stages in an Expectation-Maximization procedure. In the E-step, a convex optimization leads to a closed-form, provably optimal non-parametric variational distribution. In the M-step, the policy is improved using that distribution while remaining within a trust region. The optimality statement concerns the variational distribution computed in the first stage.

This decomposition turns policy learning into a convex optimization phase followed by a supervised learning phase, yielding more stable training. Across the reported continuous robotic tasks, the method achieves better constraint satisfaction and sample efficiency than the evaluated baselines. The practical finding is that the inference-based decomposition can improve both compliance with constraints and how efficiently experience is used.
icml-2022-constrained-variational-policy.tldr: An inference-based policy optimizer separates constrained distribution optimization from policy fitting, improving constraint satisfaction and sample efficiency in robotic experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that choose actions individually while jointly minimizing a network's total cost over time. Costs arise at individual nodes, from interactions across time, and from interactions across the network. Each agent can access predictions extending k steps ahead, but only within a neighborhood reaching r network hops away.

The proposed Localized Predictive Control algorithm adapts predictive control to this decentralized setting. Its competitive-ratio guarantee is one plus terms that decay exponentially with prediction length and neighborhood radius, up to the factors hidden by the stated notation. The decay constants lie between zero and one, and increase as the corresponding temporal or spatial interactions become stronger.

The bound quantifies how additional foresight and access to a wider neighborhood improve the guarantee, even in an adversarial setting. Stronger interactions make those improvements decay more slowly with k or r. The authors also establish lower bounds for any decentralized online algorithm, showing that their dependence on these two information resources is near optimal.
icml-2022-decentralized-online-convex-op.tldr: Localized Predictive Control achieves near-optimal dependence on prediction horizon and neighborhood radius in decentralized online convex optimization.

paragraphs: Predicting an event's probability differs from deciding whether it will happen. Training data usually provide individual outcomes, while the underlying probabilities remain unknown. This paper studies neural probability estimation from high-dimensional inputs when events have inherent uncertainty, distinguishing that problem from uncertainty caused by limited knowledge of the model.

To investigate evaluation, the authors construct synthetic data and compare metrics that can be computed from observed data. They also evaluate existing approaches on precipitation forecasting from radar images, cancer survival prediction from histopathology images, and crash prediction from dashcam videos. A theoretical model reproduces several patterns observed in these experiments.

The proposed method changes training to encourage agreement between network outputs and empirical probabilities calculated from the data. It outperforms existing approaches on most evaluated metrics across both simulated and real-world data. The contribution therefore combines an investigation of how probability estimates should be assessed with a training method aimed directly at improving those estimates, rather than only predicting individual outcomes.
icml-2022-deep-probability-estimation-ca.tldr: Training neural networks to agree with empirical probabilities improves probability estimation on most evaluated metrics in synthetic and real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Delays in observations or interactions can disrupt reinforcement learning because the information available to an agent no longer lines up with the moment when an action takes effect. This paper assumes an effective policy is already available, or can be learned easily, in the version of the environment without delays.

The proposed Delayed Imitation with Dataset Aggregation algorithm uses demonstrations from that undelayed setting to learn behavior suitable for the delayed environment. This makes imitation the bridge between a policy that works under immediate feedback and the practical task where feedback or interactions arrive late. The theoretical analysis also informs the algorithm's design.

Under smoothness conditions, the authors derive bounds relating performance in delayed and undelayed tasks. These results provide insight beyond the particular imitation algorithm, while retaining that stated condition. Experiments across robotic locomotion, classic control, and trading report strong performance with high sample efficiency. The contribution is a way to reuse undelayed competence when learning to operate with delays.
icml-2022-delayed-reinforcement-learning.tldr: DIDA learns delayed-task behavior from undelayed demonstrations, assuming an effective undelayed policy is available or easy to learn.

paragraphs: A policy learned in a simulator can become fragile when deployment conditions differ from training. This paper changes the learning objective to account for distributional changes in the environment. Instead of optimizing only for the training environment, it seeks the policy with the best performance under the worst perturbation considered by its formulation.

Directly solving this problem involves an infinite-dimensional space of possible environment perturbations. The authors transform it into a finite-dimensional dual problem, making the robust objective more manageable. They then use a multilevel Monte Carlo method to approximate the dual value from simulator samples, connecting the transformed optimization problem to a sample-based Q-learning algorithm.

The theoretical result establishes asymptotic convergence to the optimal worst-case policy. That is a convergence statement about the robust objective, rather than a claim of immediate optimality after a finite amount of training. Simulation experiments additionally report strong robustness. Together, the results support learning policies that explicitly account for the distributional environment changes represented in the problem.
icml-2022-distributionally-robust-q-lear.tldr: Distributionally robust Q-learning uses simulator samples to learn a worst-case policy and asymptotically converges to the robust optimum.

paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to learning strategies in extensive-form games. Counterfactual Regret Minimization and its variants converge quickly in practice when approximating Nash equilibria. Follow-the-Regularized-Leader and Online Mirror Descent offer an elegant optimization framework, but the abstract describes them as less practical for these games.

Earlier connections were restricted to local decision points. The authors show that CFR using Regret Matching is equivalent to a special case of FTRL, while CFR using Regret Matching+ is equivalent to a special case of OMD. These equivalences place the specified game-solving methods within broader online optimization frameworks and provide a basis for deriving new algorithms.

Using those connections, the paper develops new FTRL and OMD variants that can be viewed as extensions of vanilla CFR and CFR+. Experiments show faster convergence than conventional FTRL and OMD, and in some extensive-form games faster convergence than CFR and CFR+ themselves. The improvement over the latter methods is therefore game-dependent in the reported findings.
icml-2022-equivalence-analysis-between-c.tldr: Equivalences between specific CFR variants and FTRL or OMD yield new algorithms with improved convergence in evaluated extensive-form games.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to choose GAN latent inputs that are likely to generate high-quality images. Its starting point is hubness in high-dimensional latent spaces: some latent points typically have much higher sampling densities than others. The authors argue that these hub latents receive better training and contribute more to high-quality synthesis.

The proposed sampling method uses this hubness information to identify promising latent inputs before images are generated. That timing is central to its efficiency: selection takes place in latent space, without first synthesizing a collection of images and then choosing the most appealing outputs. The method therefore makes latent selection part of the generation procedure itself.

The authors also interpret the familiar truncation trick as a simple approximation to the tendency of hub latents to cluster centrally. This supplies a rationale for an otherwise empirical technique and motivates using hubness more directly. Extensive experiments support the proposed sampling method's effectiveness, connecting the structure of the latent distribution to the quality of generated images.
icml-2022-exploring-and-exploiting-hubne.tldr: Hubness-based sampling identifies promising GAN latent inputs before image generation and explains the truncation trick through hub clustering.

paragraphs: Fat-tailed distributions give relatively substantial probability to extreme values, creating difficulties for Gaussian-based variational approximations. This paper focuses on a further complication in multiple dimensions: tail behavior can differ depending on direction. Capturing a distribution's central region is therefore insufficient if the approximation misrepresents how probability decays away from it.

The authors strengthen theory describing how Lipschitz flows affect tail-decay rates and extend the analysis to non-Lipschitz polynomial flows. They also develop multivariate tail parameters that detect directional differences. This reveals a limitation of many existing flow-based methods: they can represent only tail-isotropic distributions, whose tail parameter is the same in every direction.

Anisotropic tail-adaptive flows are introduced to address that restriction and model targets with direction-dependent tails. Experiments on synthetic and real-world targets find the method competitive with prior work while displaying appropriate tail anisotropy. The stated finding combines competitive overall performance with the ability to express a distributional feature that many existing methods cannot capture.
icml-2022-fattailed-variational-inferenc.tldr: Anisotropic tail-adaptive flows capture direction-dependent heavy tails while remaining competitive with prior variational methods in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: In the federated setting studied here, each client labels only a small part of its data because annotation requires time and resources. A client's unlabeled examples may include several classes it does not recognize. This complicates positive-and-unlabeled learning, whose traditional setting in the abstract treats the negative category as a single class.

FedPU uses labeled information available at other clients to address those multiple unknown negative classes. Its objective is to minimize their expected risk, allowing information distributed across clients to help resolve what an individual client cannot identify from its own labels. The design directly addresses the mismatch between local labeling knowledge and the broader collection of classes.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of FedPU's generalization bound and evaluate it empirically. In the reported experiments, it performs substantially better than conventional supervised and semi-supervised federated methods. The result suggests that explicitly modeling this positive-and-unlabeled structure can be more effective than applying those conventional approaches to sparsely labeled federated data.
icml-2022-federated-learning-with-positi.tldr: FedPU uses labeled information across clients to learn from positive and unlabeled data containing multiple locally unknown negative classes.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks face a challenge when connected nodes are dissimilar, a situation called heterophily. Expanding a node's neighborhood can bring in more similar nodes, but choosing the right expansion separately for each node is difficult. Similar nodes outside the chosen neighborhood also remain unavailable for aggregation.

GloGNN and GloGNN++ instead construct node embeddings using information from across the graph. At each layer, they learn a matrix of correlations that determines how node information is combined. The coefficients can be positive or negative, and the matrix comes from an optimization problem with a closed-form solution. An accelerated aggregation procedure has linear time complexity.

The authors prove a desired grouping effect for both the coefficient matrix and the resulting embeddings, providing a theoretical account of the models' effectiveness. Experiments compare the methods with 11 competitors on 15 datasets covering varied domains, sizes, and heterophily levels. The reported results show superior performance and efficiency, supporting global aggregation as an alternative to selecting increasingly large local neighborhoods.
icml-2022-finding-global-homophily-in-gr.tldr: GloGNN and GloGNN++ learn signed global aggregation weights to exploit useful node relationships beyond local neighborhoods.

paragraphs: A blurry video frame may contain scene patches that appear sharper elsewhere in nearby frames. Recovering detail therefore requires identifying relevant information across both space and time. This paper introduces a Transformer designed for that search, addressing limitations of convolutional approaches in capturing long-range relationships and similarities between distant patches.

Its attention module uses estimated optical flow to guide the selection of information from neighboring frames. For each query in the blurry reference frame, it samples spatially sparse but closely related keys corresponding to the same scene patch. The search can reach globally across space while concentrating attention on locations identified as relevant by motion estimates.

A recurrent embedding mechanism additionally carries information from earlier frames, strengthening longer-range temporal dependencies. Together, these mechanisms combine motion-guided matching with information retained over time. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods on DVD and GOPRO, as well as visually pleasing results on real videos. The findings support targeted cross-frame information gathering for the evaluated deblurring tasks.
icml-2022-flow-guided-sparse-transformer.tldr: FGST combines optical-flow-guided sparse attention with recurrent information transfer to improve video deblurring.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions where rewards are known but the constraints governing acceptable choices are not. The motivating constraints represent human preferences that are expensive to evaluate, such as comfort and safety in driving. The learning challenge is to identify the best acceptable action while efficiently gathering information about those constraints.

The authors formulate this as constrained linear best-arm identification and propose Adaptive Constraint Learning. They derive an instance-dependent lower bound on the required samples and show that ACOL matches it in the worst case. Its average-case sample-complexity bound is also substantially tighter than those of simpler approaches, giving theoretical support for adaptive constraint learning.

In synthetic experiments, ACOL performs comparably to an oracle and better than several baselines. In a driving simulation, it learns preference constraints more sample efficiently than alternatives. The study also finds that representing preferences as constraints is more robust to scenario changes than placing them directly in the reward function, supporting this separation in the tested driving application.
icml-2022-interactively-learning-prefere.tldr: ACOL efficiently learns unknown preference constraints when rewards are known, with theoretical sample bounds and supporting driving-simulation results.

paragraphs: A treap is a randomized binary search tree with expected logarithmic access time, but its standard construction does not exploit patterns in how data are accessed. This paper augments treaps with machine advice so their structure can reflect the input distribution while continuing to support binary-search-tree operations.

The method assumes access to a frequency-estimation oracle and uses its advice to assign learned priorities to nodes. Those priorities shape the tree, making estimated access frequencies relevant to its organization. The resulting data structure supports operations including range queries and finding successors, extending learned data-structure ideas to these binary-search-tree capabilities.

The authors analyze performance under several input distributions and establish stronger guarantees than classic treaps and other traditional tree structures under the stated circumstances. Synthetic experiments show a performance advantage, and real-world experiments using known frequency-estimation oracles also show improvements. Both the theoretical and empirical contributions depend on the setting in which frequency advice is available; the abstract does not claim a distribution-independent advantage.
icml-2022-learning-augmented-binary-sear.tldr: Learning-augmented treaps use frequency predictions to shape node priorities, improving guarantees under studied distributions and performance in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Sequence models can process language at several levels of detail, but a small attention region does not necessarily correspond to a meaningful linguistic unit. This paper argues that earlier multiscale Transformers often modeled local features without respecting word boundaries. Such representations can produce redundant or ambiguous attention patterns that are difficult to interpret.

The proposed Universal MultiScale Transformer defines its scales explicitly as subwords, words, and phrases. It connects those scales using word-boundary information and prior knowledge about phrases. The approach therefore gives the hierarchy a linguistic basis, linking fine-grained pieces of text to the larger units they form rather than defining scale only through receptive-field size.

The model is evaluated on two sequence-generation tasks and achieves consistent gains over a strong baseline across several test sets without sacrificing efficiency. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating linguistic boundaries into multiscale generation models. The stated evaluation establishes performance and efficiency benefits; the interpretability concern motivates the design rather than supplying a separate quantified result in the abstract.
icml-2022-learning-multiscale-transforme.tldr: UMST links subword, word, and phrase representations using linguistic boundaries, improving evaluated sequence-generation performance without sacrificing efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper estimates how individual training examples contribute to a model's behavior, including a particular prediction. Its target quantity is the average marginal effect: the expected change from adding one example to a training subset drawn from a specified distribution. Under the uniform sampling distribution described in the abstract, this becomes the Shapley value.

The procedure resembles a randomized experiment. The authors draw different subsets of training data, train a separate submodel on each, and measure the behavior of interest. They then use LASSO regression to estimate the examples' effects jointly from which examples appeared in each subset and how the resulting submodels behaved.

The efficiency result assumes sparsity: only k of the N training examples have large average marginal effects, with k much smaller than N. Under that assumption, the estimator needs O(k log N) randomized submodel trainings, improving on prior Shapley estimators. The result makes sparse influence a computational advantage, while keeping the estimated contribution tied to the chosen distribution over training subsets.
icml-2022-measuring-the-effect-of-traini.tldr: Randomized subset training and LASSO estimate training-example contributions with O(k log N) submodel trainings under a sparse-effects assumption.

paragraphs: Online decision-making becomes harder when the cost of an action arrives only after later decisions have already been made. This paper studies that challenge for unconstrained minimization of a specially structured class of nonsubmodular functions. Its motivation includes online learning problems arising in sparse estimation and Bayesian optimization.

The authors analyze variants of online gradient descent and approximate online bandit gradient descent. They cover both full-information feedback and bandit feedback, where the information available for learning is more limited. Their guarantees address static and delayed scenarios, including cases in which the delay between a decision and its observed cost is unbounded.

The analysis uses an adapted measure called (alpha, beta)-regret and extends a convex-relaxation framework. These choices allow guarantees suited to the structured nonsubmodular problem rather than assuming ordinary convexity or submodularity. Simulation studies demonstrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The scope is the specified function class and regret formulation; allowing unbounded delays does not itself mean that delays have no effect on performance.
icml-2022-online-nonsubmodular-minimizat.tldr: The paper establishes adapted regret guarantees for structured nonsubmodular online minimization with full-information or bandit feedback, including unbounded delays.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares measures by finding how to move one into another while accounting for transportation cost. This paper adds order constraints to that formulation so a transport plan can reflect additional structure. The objective is to make the resulting solutions more explainable by incorporating structure directly into the optimization problem.

Introducing constraints also creates a computational problem: the structured formulation needs a practical solution method. The authors develop an efficient procedure for obtaining explainable solutions and report that it scales substantially better than standard approaches. They also provide theoretical properties of the method, pairing the new formulation with analysis of how it can be solved.

The experiments examine explainability on e-SNLI, a natural-language inference dataset with human-annotated rationales, and on several image color-transfer examples. In these settings, the authors find that order constraints improve explainability. The contribution thus joins a way to express structure in transport plans with a scalable method and empirical evidence from both language and image applications.
icml-2022-order-constraints-in-optimal-t.tldr: Order constraints incorporate structure into optimal transport, with an efficient solver and demonstrated explainability gains in language and image examples.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning uses estimated values to form further learning targets, so variability in those estimates can cause instability and inflate the largest target value. MeanQ addresses this source of overestimation by averaging target-value estimates across an ensemble of deep networks. Its emphasis is on reducing estimation variance to improve sample efficiency.

The authors find that five ensemble members reduce variance enough in their experiments to remove the lagging target network. This also removes that network as a source of bias and further improves sample efficiency. The paper supports its design choices through intuition and experiments, including the importance of independently sampling experience for ensemble members.

Across 26 Atari environments, MeanQ beats the strongest tested baseline, SUNRISE, in 16 environments at 100,000 interaction steps, with a reported average improvement of 68%. It also beats Rainbow DQN in 21 environments at 500,000 steps, averaging 49% improvement. Average human-level performance is reached using 200,000 plus or minus 100,000 interactions, supporting the method's sample-efficiency claim on this benchmark.
icml-2022-reducing-variance-in-temporal-.tldr: MeanQ averages ensemble value estimates to reduce variance and improve Atari sample efficiency, with five members sufficient to remove the lagging target network in experiments.

paragraphs: Question-answering benchmarks based on a fixed knowledge snapshot do not capture how a model responds when the world changes. StreamingQA instead pairs dated questions with 14 years of timestamped news articles. It includes human-written and generated questions, enabling evaluation of knowledge adaptation at particular points in time.

The authors evaluate models quarterly as they encounter articles absent from pretraining. They study both parametric models, which retain knowledge in their parameters, and semi-parametric models that also search external material. Their experiments show that parametric models can be updated without full retraining while avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

Adding new articles to a semi-parametric model's search space enables rapid adaptation, but keeping its underlying language model outdated produces worse results than using a retrained one. Parameter updates are particularly helpful for questions about more frequently occurring named entities. These findings show that refreshing searchable documents and updating the language model address related aspects of evolving knowledge, and the benchmark makes that distinction observable over time.
icml-2022-streamingqa-a-benchmark-for-ad.tldr: StreamingQA evaluates knowledge adaptation over time and shows benefits from both refreshed retrieval collections and language-model updates.

paragraphs: Teacher-student training uses an auxiliary teacher network to guide a student. It appears in knowledge distillation and in self-supervised methods whose teachers track moving averages of student parameters. TSPipe accelerates this training pattern by designing the computation schedule around the different work required by the two networks.

The key observation is that the teacher does not need a backward pass. TSPipe schedules teacher and student computations separately, interleaves their work, and relaxes dependencies to improve GPU utilization. For momentum teachers, it delays parameter updates only on the teacher side, a choice intended to preserve high model accuracy while supporting the pipeline.

The reported comparison with existing pipeline-parallelism schemes finds a better trade-off between throughput and accuracy, with throughput improvements reaching 12.15 times. That figure is the maximum reported gain, not a uniform speedup for every teacher-student workload. The contribution is a scheduling approach that uses the asymmetry between teaching and learning computations to accelerate a widely used training framework.
icml-2022-tspipe-learn-from-teacher-fast.tldr: TSPipe interleaves separately scheduled teacher and student computations, achieving better throughput–accuracy trade-offs and up to 12.15-fold higher throughput.

paragraphs: Video restoration requires understanding relationships between frames, including information separated by substantial time or displaced by motion. This paper explores sequence-to-sequence modeling for that purpose. Its premise is that sequence modeling can capture long-range dependencies, provided the method accounts for the spatial misalignment that makes video frames different from a one-dimensional language sequence.

S2SVR combines the sequence model with an unsupervised optical-flow estimator. A proposed unsupervised distillation loss trains the estimator and can alleviate data discrepancies and inaccurate flow from degraded images that affect earlier flow-based approaches. Reliable flow establishes correspondences across frames, helping the sequence model relate the same scene content at different positions.

The authors report superior performance on video deblurring, video super-resolution, and compressed-video quality enhancement. These results support combining temporal sequence modeling with motion-based alignment across several restoration tasks. The approach's significance is the connection between those components: alignment helps make the relationships the sequence model needs to learn more coherent, while sequence modeling offers a way to use information across longer frame sequences.
icml-2022-unsupervised-flow-aligned-sequ.tldr: S2SVR combines sequence-to-sequence modeling with unsupervised optical-flow alignment to improve several video-restoration tasks.
